title: Nanocomposite engineering of aggregation-induced electrochemiluminescence for biosensing and bioanalytical applications
content: Aggregation-induced electrochemiluminescence (AIECL) is a technique that integrates aggregation-induced emission (AIE) with electrochemiluminescence (ECL). By circumventing the aggregation-caused quenching (ACQ) effect inherent in conventional emitters, this approach delivers high emission efficiency and strong luminescence, which render it attractive for diagnostic and single-cell imaging applications. However, its broader adoption is constrained by several factors, including limited emission efficiency, complex synthetic routes, poor biocompatibility, a shortage of cathodic luminophores, and substantial reliance on co-reactants. Nanomaterials offer a promising means to alleviate these drawbacks. They promote controlled aggregation of AIE luminogens, amplify weak signals via multiple mechanisms such as energy/electron transfer and electromagnetic field effects, regulate energy-transfer pathways, and enable the integration of recognition and detection functionalities onto a single nanoscale entity. By addressing these fundamental issues, nanomaterial-based AIECL systems can yield marked improvements in analytical performance and considerably extend their applicability across a wide range of detection scenarios. In this review, we delineate AIECL mechanisms, elaborating on the fundamentals of AIE, ECL, and AIECL and their intrinsic synergies. We highlight the roles of nanomaterials in AIECL detection systems, inducing AIE aggregation, amplifying signals, regulating energy transfer, and multifunctional integration. We then discuss the integration of AIECL with emerging nanomaterial design and intelligent detection, which is anticipated to surmount bottlenecks to expand its application in single-cell analysis and precision medicine.
